entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Communist Party of Cuba (Partido Comunista de Cuba, PCC), established in its current form in 1965 by Fidel Castro through the merger of three revolutionary organizations (the 26th of July Movement, the Popular Socialist Party, and the Revolutionary Directorate), is the only legally recognized political party in Cuba and the governing party of the Cuban state — constitutionally designated as 'the leading force of society and the state' in Article 5 of the Cuban Constitution. The PCC has governed Cuba uninterruptedly since 1965, making it one of the world's longest-ruling governing parties.

Cuba's pre-1959 Communist Party (founded 1925) was not the revolutionary vehicle; it was Castro's 26th of July Movement — launched with the failed 1953 Moncada Barracks attack and the 1956-1959 guerrilla campaign — that overthrew Batista. Castro's ideological evolution was gradual: he did not declare Cuba socialist until April 1961 (the day before the Bay of Pigs invasion), and merged the revolutionary organizations into the PCC in 1965. The party's relationship with Moscow was close during the Cold War — Soviet subsidies (approximately $5 billion annually by 1988) kept the Cuban economy viable.

The PCC's 'Special Period' (1990-1994) following Soviet collapse saw Cuba's economy contract by 35%, requiring dramatic measures (bicycles replacing cars, urban agriculture, tourism expansion). Fidel Castro transferred power to Raúl Castro in 2008 (permanent transfer 2011); Raúl to Miguel Díaz-Canel in 2018 — the first non-Castro to lead Cuba since 1959. The 2021 anti-government protests (11J) were the largest public demonstrations since 1959, testing the party's stability.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Communist Party of Cuba — governing uninterruptedly since 1965 through Soviet subsidies, Cold War confrontation with the US, Soviet collapse, and the end of Castro family rule — represents the most durable one-party state in the Western Hemisphere and the primary test case for post-Soviet communist governance adaptation.
